episode_thesis: Recorded in the April 2025 tariff shock, the speakers argue that bonds and the dollar failed as safe havens because foreign-held US debt turns a trade war into a capital war, and that stock-bond correlation turns positive when inflation is the worry. Yo Kit argues CTAs are second responders whose crisis payoff depends on the speed of both the crisis and the CTA, that CTA diversification comes from low average beta to the first factor rather than from market count or the square root of N, that peer correlation of about 50% is stable, and that cost-aware trading uses the mean-reverting nature of trend signals; the host is more cautious about prediction, front-running and attributing impact to CTAs.

speakers.name: Yo Kit
speakers.role: Guest; systematic fixed-income/macro CTA manager (trades fixed income, discusses CTA design, diversification and costs)
speakers.speaker_note: Caption spelling 'Yo Kit' / 'Yav' is kept from the ledger; the identity is not independently confirmed here. He says he trades just fixed income in his portfolio. Ledger correction applied to C15-3: the 'many standard deviations bullish going into February' point is his.

worldview_premises.premise: A trade war can escalate into a capital war because foreigners own about 30% of US debt and about $2 trillion must be refinanced each year; a Treasury rout is intolerable for policymakers.
worldview_premises.support: Debt ownership and refinancing facts; France's statement; the 10-year auction; timing of the tariff pause

worldview_premises.premise: When inflation is the concern, stocks and bonds are positively correlated, so 60/40 cannot rely on bonds; when one factor drives commodities, equities and bonds, CTAs are a needed diversifier.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of April 2025 and 2022

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers have positive convexity over months but negative skew day to day in each asset class, so a day-one cross-asset shock cannot be adjusted away; the defence is rigorous risk management.
worldview_premises.support: Practitioner experience

worldview_premises.premise: CTAs lose when speed of the crisis outruns speed of CTAs: the industry migrated from faster models in the early 2000s to 1-3 month speeds, so it keeps residual equity longs into a fast crash from an all-time high.
worldview_premises.support: SG CTA index behaviour; industry speed migration

worldview_premises.premise: CTAs risk-manage aggressively, so after a sharp sell-off they cut risk and miss the rebound.
worldview_premises.support: Own practice; sees across-the-board risk cuts

worldview_premises.premise: CTA diversification is the volatility-reduction factor, dominated by the average market beta to the first principal factor, not by the number of markets or the square root of N; low-correlation markets (metals, some energy) matter most.
worldview_premises.support: Worked example with 100 stocks at 30% beta (index risk $30 versus idiosyncratic under $10); Quantica paper

worldview_premises.premise: Capacity limits can be converted into alpha and into differentiation: smaller managers can trade low-correlation commodity markets at meaningful size.
worldview_premises.support: Argument; Quantica paper

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity trend markets are the most consistent performers in equity crises.
worldview_premises.support: Earlier study (unnamed) he recalls

worldview_premises.premise: CTAs are highly loaded on the same first factor (about 70% loading, 50% pairwise correlation, stable since 2011), which shows momentum is a macro factor and the trend engine still works.
worldview_premises.support: CFM note; Goldman paper (about 60% for CTAs versus about 30% for macro managers)

worldview_premises.premise: Trend works because returns are autocorrelated, and the payoff is like buying an option at realised rather than implied vol.
worldview_premises.support: Data going back hundreds of years

worldview_premises.premise: Trend predictors are mean-reverting (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-like): the stronger the signal, the stronger the pull back to zero, so at high signal strength costs matter more; breakout systems differ.
worldview_premises.support: Mathematical model of signals

worldview_premises.premise: There are two sources of trend alpha, long-term secular trend and short-term autocorrelation, and predictor design should match what is harvested in each market and the cost.
worldview_premises.support: Argument from Moritz's Substack dispersion of predictors (100% to 400%)

decision_process.why: Know thyself and incorporate cost, not predict price

decision_process.practice: Rigorous day-one risk management because a cross-asset shock cannot be diversified away.
Overweight low-beta, less correlated markets (commodities) and accept capacity limits.
decision_process.why: Reduce beta to the first factor

decision_process.practice: Choose predictor design by what is harvested (secular trend versus short-term autocorrelation) and cost; mix of predictors.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following depends on time as well as price: moves that have not lasted long enough do not flip long-lookback models.

worldview_premises.premise: Vol explosions cut positions even faster than signals; the extra volatility seen at trend exhaustion cannot be attributed to CTAs alone.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The causal claim that the bond rout forced the tariff pause is Yo Kit's inference ('probably'), not shown.
Speaker attribution of C15-3 was mixed; the ledger correction splits it between host and guest.
The host expected large dispersion in April 2025 but the cited CFM and Goldman data concern historical pairwise correlations; no April 2025 dispersion data are shown.
Quoted statistics (Tyler Loving's study, mid-April index performance, 3-day yield jump) are from memory or partial-month data, and the host warns they are not final.
The 'diversification factor 3 turns 0.25 into 0.75' example and the beta-to-first-factor argument are made for stocks and transferred by analogy to CTAs without CTA-specific numbers.
Commodity-in-crisis consistency relies on an unnamed earlier study; April 2025 evidence is partial (gold, energy).
Source of 5-10% vol-forecast accuracy from trend level is not documented.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs the speakers treat as leading: US long-end yields and auction results, foreign demand for Treasuries, dollar and cross-country yield dispersion, stock-bond correlation (inflation regime), vol spikes (cause synchronous CTA de-risking), the speed of equity drawdowns relative to model lookbacks, and the duration of declines for signal flips. Horizon is days to weeks for CTA flows and months for trend response; no price targets are given.
reader_inferences: (reader) The 'second responder' point and Yo Kit's industry-speed migration imply that CTA crisis alpha depends on the crisis's duration relative to 1-3 month lookbacks, so fast V-shaped events are structurally unfavourable.

(reader) Yo Kit's diversification argument implies that low-beta markets matter more than breadth, which is in tension with the host's own large-commodity-set practice only in emphasis, not in direction.
(reader) Both speakers treat vol-targeted de-risking as a source of crowded exits, so CTA drawdowns in sharp reversals are partly self-inflicted by the same sizing rule that controls risk.
(reader) The mean-reversion-of-signal argument for cost control could make execution rules path-dependent; the host's type I / type II concern suggests it needs out-of-sample testing.
